en.title: What has already happened
en.goal: Talk about completed actions, changes of state, and what hasn't happened yet.

lessons.nao-aconteceu: Talking about what didn't happen yesterday

phrases.t: I don't want to eat anymore.
I didn't go to work yesterday.

dialogue.title: Have you eaten?
lines: I've eaten, I ate two apples.
I didn't have dinner yesterday, so I'm very hungry today.

le-completion.title: 了 (le) — marking completion
le-completion.body: 了 (le) after a verb shows that the action was completed — it works somewhat like the English simple past ("I ate"). The structure is: Verb + 了 + Object.

buxiang-le.title: 不想...了 — "don't want anymore"
buxiang-le.body: When 不 (or 没) is combined with 了 at the end of the sentence, the meaning becomes "no longer" — showing that something that was happening or was true has stopped.
examples: I don't want to eat anymore

le-question.title: 了...吗 — asking whether something has already happened
le-question.body: To ask whether an action has already been completed, you combine 了 (marking completion) with 吗 (marking a question) at the end of the sentence — together they ask "has that happened yet?".

chifanle-greeting.title: "你吃饭了吗？" is sometimes not a real question
chifanle-greeting.body: Besides literally asking whether someone has eaten, 你吃了吗？ (the short version, without 饭) is traditionally used as a greeting — something like "how are you?" in English, without expecting a detailed answer about food. It's a more cultural/traditional use than a universal one today, but it's worth recognizing when you hear it.
examples: how are you? (traditional greeting, not a literal question)

haimei.title: Why does "wǒ hái méi chī" never take "le"?
haimei.body: 了 marks a completed action. But in the negative with hái méi (还没, not yet), the le disappears — never "wǒ hái méi chī le". It makes sense: if the action hasn't happened yet, there's nothing to mark as completed.

meiyou-past.title: 没有 + verb — negating the past
meiyou-past.body: To say that something didn't happen in the past, Chinese puts 没有 (or just 没) before the verb — never 不, which is reserved for negating the present or the future.
examples: I didn't go to work yesterday

bu-vs-mei.title: 不 vs. 没 — two negations, two times
bu-vs-mei.body: 不 (bù) negates the present and the future — what isn't or won't be. 没 (méi) negates the past — what didn't happen. One important exception: the verb 是 is never negated with 没, always with 不, even when talking about the past.
examples: I didn't go to work yesterday (past)

le-bridge.title: The same 了 again, with a different role
le-bridge.body: Remember "你怎么了？" (what's wrong with you?) back in Unit 11? There, 了 marked a change of state. Here, 了 after the verb marks a completed action. It's the same particle with two different roles — the context (end of the sentence vs. right after the verb) tells you which is which.
examples: what's wrong with you? (change of state)

shide-deferred.title: 是...的 — emphasizing how something happened
shide-deferred.body: Remember "Nǐ shì zěnme lái de?" (how did you come?) back in Unit 10? Now that you know Chinese marks completed actions, this construction makes more sense: 是...的 emphasizes a specific detail (manner, place or time) of an action that has already been completed — which is why the question uses this structure and not an ordinary question.
examples: how did you come? (emphasis on the manner)
